nodes.title: Companies Act
nodes.authority: Ministry of Corporate Affairs / India Code

nodes.content: Formation of Company: A company may be formed for any lawful purpose by seven or more persons (Public Company), two or more persons (Private Company), or one person (One Person Company / OPC).

Incorporation of Company: Documents including Memorandum of Association (MOA) and Articles of Association (AOA) signed by subscribers, declaration by professionals, and details of directors shall be filed with the Registrar of Companies (ROC) for incorporation certificate.

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR): Every company having net worth of rupees five hundred crore or more, or turnover of rupees one thousand crore or more, or net profit of rupees five crore or more during immediately preceding financial year shall constitute a CSR Committee and ensure that company spends in every financial year at least two per cent (2%) of average net profits made during three immediately preceding financial years on CSR activities.

Company to have Board of Directors: Every company shall have a Board of Directors consisting of individuals. Minimum 3 directors for public company, 2 for private company, 1 for OPC. Maximum 15 directors. Every listed public company shall have at least one-third of total directors as independent directors.

Duties of Directors: A director of a company shall act in accordance with articles, act in good faith to promote objects of company for benefit of members, exercise duties with due and reasonable care, skill and diligence, not involve in situation of conflict of interest, and not achieve undue gain or advantage.

Application to Tribunal for relief in cases of oppression: Any member of a company who complains that affairs of company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or oppressive to him or any member may apply to National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).
This Act may be called the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. It replaces the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. It extends to the whole of India.

Definitions: 'Consumer' means any person who buys any goods or hires/avails any services for a consideration, including offline and online transactions (e-commerce), but does not include a person who obtains goods for resale or commercial purpose. 'Consumer rights' include the right to be protected against marketing of goods/services hazardous to life/property, right to be informed about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price, right to be assured access to variety at competitive

Establishment of Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA): Central Government shall establish a Central Authority to promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a class, and to regulate matters relating to violation of rights of consumers, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements which are prejudicial to the interests of public and consumers.

Power of Central Authority to issue directions and penalties against false or misleading advertisements: CCPA may issue directions to trader, manufacturer, endorser, advertiser or publisher to discontinue or modify misleading ads, and impose penalty up to ten lakh rupees, and for subsequent offence up to fifty lakh rupees.

District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (District Commission): Established in each district. Jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed fifty lakh rupees (up to Rs. 50 Lakhs).

State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (State Commission): Established in each State. Jurisdiction to entertain complaints where consideration paid exceeds fifty lakh rupees but does not exceed two crore rupees (Rs. 50 Lakhs to Rs. 2 Crores), and appeals against District Commission orders.

National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (National Commission): Established at national level. Jurisdiction to entertain complaints where consideration paid exceeds two crore rupees (exceeding Rs. 2 Crores), and appeals against State Commission orders.

Product Liability Action: A complainant may bring a product liability action against a product manufacturer, product service provider, or product seller for any harm caused to him on account of a defective product or deficient service.

Interpretation clause: (a) Proposal: When one person signifies to another his willingness to do or abstain from doing anything with a view to obtaining the assent of that other. (b) Acceptance: When the person to whom proposal is made signifies assent. (e) Agreement: Every promise and every set of promises, forming consideration for each other. (h) Contract: An agreement enforceable by law is a contract.

What agreements are contracts: All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.

Who are competent to contract: Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law.

Free consent defined: Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by coercion (Section 15), undue influence (Section 16), fraud (Section 17), misrepresentation (Section 18), or mistake (Sections 20, 21, 22).

Agreement in restraint of trade void: Every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind, is to that extent void, except in sale of goodwill.

Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract: When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach (Hadley v Baxendale rule). Remote or indirect damage is not compensable.

Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for: When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach (liquidated damages or penalty), the party complaining of breach is entitled to receive reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named.
'Contract of indemnity' defined: A contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself, or by the conduct of any other person.

'Contract of guarantee', 'surety', 'principal debtor' and 'creditor': A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. The person who gives guarantee is 'surety'.
The Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 extends to the whole of India and applies to all offenses under the Indian Penal Code and other laws.
All offenses under the Indian Penal Code shall be investigated, inquired into, tried, and otherwise dealt with according to the provisions of this Code.
Criminal courts include: Supreme Court, High Courts, Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates of First Class, Second Class, and Executive Magistrates.
The High Court establishes Courts of Session presided over by a Sessions Judge appointed by the High Court.
In every district, the Chief Judicial Magistrate is appointed who exercises supervision over other Judicial Magistrates.
Judicial Magistrates of the First Class are appointed in every district by the High Court.
Any offense not punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment exceeding 7 years may be tried by a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.
A Judicial Magistrate of the Second Class may try offenses punishable with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine up to Rs. 5000.
A Court of Session may pass any sentence authorized by law, but any death sentence must be confirmed by the High Court.
A Chief Judicial Magistrate may pass any sentence except death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment exceeding 7 years.
A police officer may arrest without warrant any person concerned in a cognizable offense, or against whom a reasonable complaint has been made.
In cases where arrest is not necessary, the police officer shall issue a notice of appearance. If the person complies, no arrest shall be made.
In making an arrest, the police officer shall actually touch or confine the body of the person unless there is submission to custody by word or action.
A police officer may break open any door or window to enter and search any place if entry is otherwise impossible, after giving notice of purpose.
Every person arrested without warrant shall be informed of the full particulars of the offense for which he is arrested immediately.
A police officer making an arrest shall produce the arrested person before a magistrate without unnecessary delay, within 24 hours.
No person arrested shall be detained for more than 24 hours without being produced before a magistrate.
Arrest shall not be made unnecessarily and no more restraint than necessary shall be used.
Summons shall be in writing, signed by the presiding officer, and shall state the offense charged.
Every summons shall be served by a police officer or public servant by delivering a copy to the person summoned.
Where the person cannot be found, the summons may be served by leaving a copy with an adult family member.
Where there is no reasonable likelihood of personal service, the serving officer may affix a copy of the summons to the outer door of the residence.
Service by post is permissible in certain cases where the court deems it fit.
A warrant of arrest shall be signed by the presiding officer and shall bear the seal of the court.
Every warrant of arrest shall be directed to one or more police officers, requiring them to arrest the person named.
A warrant may be directed to any person for execution outside the local jurisdiction of the court.
If a person absconds to avoid warrant, the court may publish a proclamation requiring his appearance.
After proclamation, the court may order attachment of the absconder's property.
A court may issue a summons for the production of any document or other thing necessary for investigation or trial.
The court may summon a public servant to produce a public document in his custody.
A search warrant may be issued where the court has reason to believe a person will not produce a document or thing.
Search warrants may be issued for search of a place suspected to contain stolen property, forged documents, or evidence of an offense.
A magistrate may issue a search warrant for a person wrongfully confined.
When a search is conducted, the officer shall call upon independent witnesses and shall prepare a list of all things seized.
A court may require a person convicted of certain offenses to execute a bond to keep the peace for a period not exceeding 3 years.
When a magistrate receives information that a person is likely to commit a breach of peace or disturb public tranquility, he may require a bond for keeping the peace.
Security for good behavior may be required from persons disseminating seditious matter or promoting class hatred.
Security may be required from persons suspected of concealing a design to commit a cognizable offense.
Security may be required from habitual offenders, robbers, thieves, and persons who are a danger to society.
A police officer may prevent any injury attempted to be caused to any public property.
A police officer may intervene to prevent the commission of cognizable offenses.
A police officer knowing of a design to commit a cognizable offense shall arrest the person without order from a magistrate.
A magistrate may issue orders in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger, directing a person to abstain from a certain act or to take order with property in his possession.
A magistrate may make orders to prevent disputes concerning land or water likely to cause a breach of peace.
If a person having sufficient means neglects to maintain his wife, children, or parents who are unable to maintain themselves, a magistrate may order monthly maintenance of up to Rs. 5000.
Proceedings under Section 125 may be taken against any person in any district where he resides or where his wife resides.
An order under Section 125 may be altered or modified on proof of change in circumstances.
A magistrate may enforce payment of maintenance by issuing a warrant for levying the amount due.

Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offense given orally to a police officer shall be reduced to writing and signed by the informant. This is the First Information Report (FIR). A copy shall be given free of cost to the informant.
Information relating to non-cognizable offenses shall be entered in a diary and the police officer shall refer the informant to the magistrate.
A police officer may investigate any cognizable offense without the order of a magistrate.
If a police officer has reason to suspect the commission of a cognizable offense, he shall send a report to the magistrate and proceed to investigate.
A police officer may require attendance of witnesses acquainted with the facts for examination during investigation.
A police officer may examine orally any person supposed to be acquainted with the facts. The person is bound to answer truly except incriminating questions.
No statement made to a police officer during investigation shall be signed, and it may be used only for contradicting the witness in court.
A magistrate may record any confession or statement made during investigation. Confessions recorded under this section are admissible in evidence.

If investigation cannot be completed within 24 hours, the accused shall be produced before a magistrate who may authorize detention for up to 15 days. Total judicial custody may extend up to 90 days for serious offenses and 60 days for others.
If upon investigation there is no sufficient evidence, the police shall release the accused on bond.
If sufficient evidence is found, the police shall forward the accused to a magistrate for trial.
On completion of investigation, the police shall submit a final report (charge sheet) to the magistrate with all relevant documents.
Every offense shall ordinarily be tried by a court within whose local jurisdiction it was committed.
Where the offense consists of several acts done in different local areas, the trial may be in any such area.
Where an act is done in one place and the consequence ensues in another, the trial may be in either place.
Where it is uncertain in which jurisdiction an offense was committed, the trial may be in any such area.
A magistrate may take cognizance of an offense upon receiving a complaint, upon a police report, or upon information from any person.
A court shall not take cognizance of offenses against public justice or contempt of lawful authority except on complaint in writing by the concerned court.
For certain offenses against the State, cognizance may be taken only with prior sanction of the central or state government.
A magistrate taking cognizance of an offense on complaint shall examine the complainant upon oath and reduce the substance to writing.
The magistrate may postpone issuance of process and conduct an inquiry or direct investigation by police.
If the magistrate finds no sufficient ground for proceeding, he shall dismiss the complaint.
Every charge shall state the offense with which the accused is charged, giving the name and specific provision of law.
The charge shall contain particulars as to time, place, and person against whom the offense was committed.
For every distinct offense, there shall be a separate charge and each charge shall be tried separately.
When a person is charged with an offense and facts prove a minor offense, he may be convicted of the minor offense.
If the judge finds grounds for presuming the accused committed the offense, he shall frame a charge in writing.
When the accused is brought before the Court of Session, the prosecution shall open its case by describing the charge and stating the evidence.
If the judge finds no sufficient ground for proceeding, he shall discharge the accused.
The prosecution shall produce its evidence after the charge is read and explained.
If after prosecution evidence the judge finds no evidence against the accused, he shall record an acquittal.
Where the accused is not acquitted, he shall enter his defense and produce evidence.
After hearing arguments, the judge shall give judgment. If convicted, the judge shall hear the accused on sentence.
If the magistrate finds the accused not guilty, he shall acquit. If guilty, he shall convict and pass sentence.
In warrant cases instituted on police report, the magistrate shall satisfy himself that the documents have been furnished to the accused.
If the magistrate considers the charge groundless, he shall discharge the accused.
If the magistrate finds reason to proceed, he shall frame a charge in writing against the accused.
The prosecution shall produce evidence after the charge is framed. The magistrate may issue summons to witnesses.
The accused may produce evidence in defense after the prosecution closes its case.
If the complainant is absent, the magistrate may acquit the accused or adjourn the case.
If a complaint is found false or vexatious, the magistrate may order compensation to the accused.
In summons cases, the magistrate shall state the particulars of the offense to the accused and ask if he pleads guilty.
If the accused pleads guilty, the magistrate shall record the plea and convict him.
In petty cases, the magistrate may convict the accused on his plea of guilty without trial.
If the accused does not plead guilty, the magistrate shall hear the prosecution evidence and the accused's evidence.
If the magistrate finds the accused not guilty, he shall acquit. If guilty, he shall pass sentence.
In summons cases, the complainant may withdraw the complaint, and the magistrate shall acquit the accused.
In summons cases, the magistrate may stop proceedings and discharge the accused at any stage without recording an acquittal.
The following offenses may be tried summarily: offenses punishable with imprisonment up to 2 years, theft, receiving stolen property, criminal trespass, etc.
In summary trials, no sentence of imprisonment exceeding 3 months shall be passed.
The magistrate shall maintain a brief record of the substance of evidence and particulars of conviction.
A person arrested for a non-bailable offense shall be released on bail if the offense is bailable. The police officer shall release him on executing a bond.
A person accused of a non-bailable offense may be released on bail, except where there are reasonable grounds to believe guilt of an offense punishable with death or life imprisonment.
A High Court or Court of Session may grant bail to any person accused of any offense, including non-bailable offenses.
The amount of bail shall be fixed with due regard to the circumstances and shall not be excessive.
Before a person is released on bail, a bond for the sum fixed shall be executed.
A court may accept a deposit of money or valuable property in lieu of a bond.
If bail is forfeited, the bond and any surety amount shall be forfeited to the government.
No appeal shall lie from a judgment of acquittal unless the State government directs an appeal. The victim also has a right to appeal.
Appeals from convictions by the Court of Session lie to the High Court. Appeals from magistrate convictions lie to the Sessions Court.
No appeal lies where the accused pleads guilty and is convicted on such plea, except as to the extent or legality of the sentence.
No appeal lies in petty cases where the magistrate imposes a fine only of up to Rs. 100.
The State government may appeal against the inadequacy of sentence to the High Court.
The State government may appeal against an acquittal to the High Court.
After hearing an appeal, the appellate court may reverse, confirm, or modify the judgment, or order a new trial.
Pending appeal, the appellate court may suspend the sentence and release the appellant on bail.
A Sessions Judge may refer a question of law arising in a case to the High Court.
The High Court or Sessions Judge may call for and examine the records of any inferior criminal court to satisfy themselves on the correctness or legality of any finding, sentence or order.
The High Court may exercise revision powers suo motu or on application. No revision lies against an order of acquittal.
The power of revision shall not be exercised in favor of the convicted person unless an opportunity of being heard is given to the prosecution.

Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any court, or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.
This Act may be called the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. It was enacted in the wake of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy to provide for the protection and improvement of environment.

Power of Central Government to take measures to protect and improve environment: Central Government shall have the power to take all such measures as it deems necessary or expedient for protecting environment and preventing environmental pollution, including setting standards for quality of environment, emission of pollutants, and restriction of industrial areas.

Power to give directions: Central Government may in exercise of its powers issue directions in writing to any person, officer or authority and such person or authority shall be bound to comply. Includes power to direct closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry or stoppage of electricity or water supply.

Persons carrying on industry, operation, etc., not to allow discharge or emission of environmental pollutants in excess of standards: No person carrying on any industry, operation or process shall discharge or emit or permit to be discharged any environmental pollutant in excess of prescribed standards.

Penalty for contravention of provisions of Act, Rules, Orders and Directions: Whoever fails to comply with or contravenes any provision of this Act shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years or with fine which may extend to one lakh rupees, or with both.

Evidence means and includes all statements which the court permits or requires to be made before it by witnesses relating to matters of fact under inquiry. Documents produced for inspection are also evidence.
Evidence may be given in any suit or proceeding of the existence or non-existence of every fact in issue and of such other facts as are declared to be relevant.
Facts which form part of the same transaction are relevant whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places.
Facts which are the occasion, cause, or effect of relevant facts are relevant.
Any fact is relevant which shows or constitutes a motive, preparation, or previous or subsequent conduct.
Facts necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue or relevant fact, or to rebut an inference, or to establish identity, are relevant.
Facts not otherwise relevant are relevant if they are inconsistent with any fact in issue or relevant fact, or if they make the existence of any fact in issue highly probable or improbable.
Facts showing the existence of any state of mind, such as intention, knowledge, good faith, negligence, or rashness, are relevant.
Facts bearing on the question whether an act was accidental or intentional are relevant.
An admission is a statement suggesting any inference as to a fact in issue or relevant fact, made by a party to the proceeding.
Statements made by a party to the proceeding, or by an agent authorized, are admissions.
A confession made by an accused person is irrelevant in criminal proceedings if it appears to have been caused by inducement, threat or promise.
No confession made to a police officer shall be proved against a person accused of any offense.
No confession made by a person while in custody of a police officer shall be proved unless made in the immediate presence of a magistrate.
When any fact is discovered in consequence of information received from a person in custody, so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved.
A confession made after the removal of inducement, threat or promise is relevant.

Statements of persons who are dead or cannot be found are relevant when they relate to the cause of death (dying declaration), or are made in the ordinary course of business, or against the pecuniary interest of the maker.
Whoever desires a court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts must prove that those facts exist.
The burden of proof lies on the person who would fail if no evidence were given on either side.
The burden of proof as to any particular fact lies on the person who wishes the court to believe in its existence.
The burden of proving any fact necessary to be proved to make evidence admissible lies on the person who wishes to give such evidence.
The burden of proving the existence of circumstances bringing the case within any exception or proviso is on the accused.
When any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon him.
When the question is whether a person was alive or dead, and it is shown that he was alive within the last 30 years, the burden of proving his death is on the person who asserts it.
If a person has not been heard of for 7 years by those who would naturally have heard, the burden of proving he is alive is on the person who asserts it.
A child born during the continuance of a valid marriage, or within 280 days after dissolution, shall be conclusive proof of legitimacy.
Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman: if within 7 years of marriage she commits suicide and was subjected to cruelty, the court may presume the husband abetted suicide.
Presumption as to dowry death: if within 7 years of marriage a woman dies under unnatural circumstances and was subjected to dowry cruelty, the court shall presume dowry death.

When a person has by his declaration, act or omission intentionally caused another to believe a thing to be true and to act upon that belief, neither he nor his representative shall be allowed to deny the truth of that thing.
A tenant of immovable property or a person who came upon land by license is estopped from denying the title of the landlord or licensor.
The acceptor of a bill of exchange is estopped from denying the drawer's authority or the existence of the payee.

All persons shall be competent to testify unless the court considers they are prevented from understanding questions or giving rational answers due to tender years, extreme old age, disease of mind, or any other cause.
Witnesses who cannot speak may give evidence by writing or by signs.
In civil proceedings, the husband or wife of a party is a competent witness.
No judge or magistrate shall be compelled to answer questions about his own conduct in court as a judge or magistrate.
No person who is or has been married shall be compelled to disclose any communication made during marriage.
No person shall be permitted to give evidence derived from unpublished official records relating to affairs of State, except with the permission of the head of the department.
No public officer shall be compelled to disclose communications made to him in official confidence when he considers that the public interest would suffer.
A witness shall not be excused from answering questions on the ground that the answer will incriminate him. However, such answers shall not subject him to arrest or prosecution.
An accomplice shall be a competent witness against an accused person; however, a conviction is not illegal merely because it proceeds on the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice.
No particular number of witnesses shall be required for the proof of any fact.
The order in which witnesses are produced and examined shall be regulated by the court.
When either party proposes to give evidence of any fact, the judge may ask how the fact is relevant. The judge shall admit the evidence if it is relevant.
The examination of a witness includes examination-in-chief by the party who calls him, cross-examination by the adverse party, and re-examination by the party who called him.
Witnesses shall be first examined-in-chief, then cross-examined, then re-examined. The court may permit cross-examination at any stage.
A leading question is one that suggests the answer desired by the person asking it.
Leading questions may not be asked in examination-in-chief without the court's permission, except on introductory or undisputed matters.
Leading questions may be asked in cross-examination.
A witness may be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing or reduced to writing, without showing the writing to him.
In cross-examination, questions may be put to test the veracity of the witness, to discover his position in life, or to shake his credit.
If a question is asked only to insult or annoy, the court shall forbid it.
The credit of a witness may be impeached by evidence of his unworthiness of belief, or by proof of inconsistent statements.
A witness may refresh his memory by referring to any writing made by himself or under his direction at the time of the transaction.
The contents of documents may be proved either by primary or secondary evidence.
Primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the court.
Secondary evidence includes certified copies, copies made from the original by mechanical processes, copies made from or compared with the original, and oral accounts of contents.
Documents must be proved by primary evidence except in the cases excepted by the Act.
Secondary evidence may be given when the original is lost, destroyed, in possession of the adversary, or when it is a public document.
Public documents include documents forming the acts or records of sovereign authority, official bodies, tribunals, and public officers.
All documents other than public documents are private documents.
Every person has a right to inspect and obtain certified copies of public documents.
Certified copies may be produced in place of the original public document.
The court shall presume every document purporting to be a certified copy to be genuine if it appears to be a correct copy of the original.
The court shall presume any document purporting to be a record of evidence or judgment to be genuine.
The court shall presume the genuineness of every document purporting to be a Gazette, newspaper, or government publication.
The court shall presume the genuineness of every electronic record purporting to be an official record.
The court shall presume that a document 30 years old (produced from proper custody) is genuine and was signed by the person it purports to be signed by.

nodes.content: Goods and Services Tax Council (Article 279A): President shall constitute GST Council. Union Finance Minister is Chairperson. GST Council makes recommendations to Union and States on taxes, cesses, exemptions, model GST laws, and GST rates.
nodes.act: Central Goods and Services Tax Act

nodes.content: Scope of Supply: For purposes of this Act, 'supply' includes all forms of supply of goods or services or both such as sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal made or agreed to be made for a consideration by a person in the course or furtherance of business.
nodes.act: Central Goods and Services Tax Act

nodes.content: Levy and Collection: There shall be levied a tax called the central goods and services tax (CGST) on all intra-State supplies of goods or services or both, except on supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption, at rates specified on recommendation of Council.
nodes.act: Central Goods and Services Tax Act

nodes.content: Eligibility and conditions for taking Input Tax Credit (ITC): Every registered person shall be entitled to take credit of input tax charged on any supply of goods or services to him which are used in furtherance of business. Conditions: possession of tax invoice, receipt of goods/services, tax paid to Government, valid return filed.
nodes.act: Central Goods and Services Tax Act

nodes.content: Persons liable for registration: Every supplier shall be liable to be registered under this Act in State or Union territory from where he makes taxable supply if aggregate turnover in a financial year exceeds twenty lakh rupees (Rs. 20 Lakhs for services / Rs. 40 Lakhs for goods in specified States).

nodes.content: This Act shall be called the Indian Penal Code (1860). It extends to the whole of India.
Every person shall be liable to punishment under this Code for every act or omission contrary to its provisions, committed within India.
Any person liable by Indian law for an offense committed outside India shall be dealt with according to Indian law.
The Code applies to any citizen of India for any offense committed outside India, and to any person on a ship or aircraft registered in India.
Throughout the Code every definition of an offense, every penal provision, and every illustration is subject to the exceptions contained in Chapter IV.
The expression 'gender' denotes the male gender, but references to the masculine include females unless context otherwise requires.
The word 'person' includes any company, association, or body of persons, whether incorporated or not.
'Public servant' includes every officer in the military, navy or air force, judge, officer of a court of justice, police officer, and every officer whose duty is to prevent offenses.
'Movable property' includes corporeal property of every description, except land and things attached to the earth.
'Dishonestly' means doing anything with the intention of causing wrongful gain or wrongful loss.
'Fraudulently' means doing anything with the intent to defraud but not otherwise.
'Reason to believe' means a person has sufficient cause to believe a thing but not otherwise.
Punishments under the Code include: Death, imprisonment for life, imprisonment (rigorous or simple), forfeiture of property, and fine.
In every sentence of death, the appropriate government may commute the punishment without the consent of the offender.
The appropriate government may commute a sentence of imprisonment for life to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 14 years.
In calculating fractions of terms of imprisonment, imprisonment for life shall be reckoned as equivalent to imprisonment for 20 years.
Where no sum is expressed to which a fine may extend, the amount of fine to which the offender is liable is unlimited but shall not be excessive.
In default of payment of fine, the offender shall undergo imprisonment of either description for a term as per the court's discretion.
Nothing is an offense done by a person who is bound by law to do it or who by reason of a mistake of fact in good faith believes himself bound by law to do it.
Nothing is an offense done by a person who by reason of a mistake of fact in good faith believes himself justified by law in doing it.
Nothing is an offense if done by accident or misfortune, without any criminal intention or knowledge, in the doing of a lawful act in a lawful manner.

Nothing is an offense merely by reason of its being done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it was done without criminal intent to cause harm and in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm.
Nothing is an offense done by a child under 7 years of age.
Nothing is an offense done by a child above 7 and under 12 years, who has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the consequences.
Nothing is an offense done by a person who, at the time of doing it, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act due to unsoundness of mind.
Nothing is an offense done by a person who was intoxicated against his will.
In cases where an act requires a particular intent or knowledge, the state of intoxication shall be taken into account.
Nothing is an offense if done by consent, where no harm is intended or likely, and the harm done does not amount to grievous hurt or death.
Nothing is an offense done in good faith for the benefit of a person who has given consent, even if the act causes harm.
Nothing is an offense done in the exercise of the right of private defense.

Every person has a right to defend their own body and the body of any other person against any offense affecting the human body, and to defend their own or another's property against theft, robbery, mischief, or criminal trespass.

The right of private defense of the body extends to causing death when the attack reasonably causes apprehension of death, grievous hurt, assault with intent to rape, kidnapping, or wrongful confinement.

The right of private defense of property extends to causing death when the offense is robbery, house-breaking by night, mischief by fire on a building, theft or mischief where there is reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
A person abets the doing of a thing when he instigates, engages in conspiracy, or intentionally aids the doing of that thing.
An abettor is a person who abets either the commission of an offense or the commission of an act which would be an offense if done by a person capable by law.
Whoever abets any offense shall be punished with the punishment provided for the offense if the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment.
Whoever abets the commission of an offense punishable with death or imprisonment for life shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
When two or more persons agree to do an illegal act or a legal act by illegal means, such an agreement is a criminal conspiracy.

Whoever is a party to a criminal conspiracy shall be punished with imprisonment up to 6 months or fine or both for minor conspiracies, or the same punishment as for the offense conspired for serious offenses.
Whoever wages war against the Government of India, or attempts to wage war, or abets the waging of such war, shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life and fine.
Whoever by words, signs, or visible representation brings or attempts to bring into hatred or contempt the Government of India shall be punished with imprisonment for life or up to 3 years and fine.
Whoever abets the committing of mutiny by an officer, soldier, sailor or airman shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life or up to 10 years and fine.
An unlawful assembly is an assembly of 5 or more persons with a common object to use criminal force, commit mischief, or intimidate.
Whoever joins an unlawful assembly shall be punished with imprisonment up to 6 months or fine or both.
Whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly, every member is guilty of rioting.
Whoever is guilty of rioting shall be punished with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both.
Every member of an unlawful assembly is guilty of any offense committed by any member in prosecution of the common object.
Whoever promotes enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, or language shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.
An affray is committed when two or more persons fight in a public place to the terror of the public.
Whoever, being a public servant, knowingly disobeys any law with intent to cause injury to any person shall be punished with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine or both.
Whoever, being a public servant, frames an incorrect document with intent to cause injury shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.
Whoever absconds to avoid service of summons or other proceedings shall be punished with imprisonment up to 1 month or fine or both.
Whoever, being bound by law to attend as a witness, intentionally omits to attend, shall be punished with imprisonment up to 6 months or fine or both.
Whoever, being legally bound by oath or by express provision of law to state the truth, makes a false statement, is said to give false evidence.
Whoever intentionally gives false evidence shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
Whoever causes evidence of an offense to disappear, or gives false information to screen the offender, shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years.
Whoever, knowing or having reason to believe that an offense has been committed, intentionally omits to give information thereof, shall be punished with imprisonment up to 6 months or fine or both.
Whoever secretes or destroys any document which he is legally bound to produce as evidence shall be punished with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both.
Whoever institutes criminal proceedings with false charges intending to cause injury shall be punished with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both.
'Coin' means metal used as money, stamped and issued by the Government to be used as currency.
Whoever counterfeits or performs any part of the process of counterfeiting coin shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
Whoever fraudulently uses any false weight or false measure shall be punished with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine or both.
A person is guilty of a public nuisance who does any act or omits to take care which causes common injury, danger or annoyance to the public.
Whoever unlawfully or negligently does any act likely to spread infection of any disease dangerous to life shall be punished with imprisonment up to 6 months or fine or both.
Whoever drives any vehicle on a public way rashly or negligently so as to endanger human life shall be punished with imprisonment up to 6 months or fine or both.
Whoever sells, distributes, or exhibits obscene material shall be punished with imprisonment up to 2 years and fine on first conviction.
Whoever does any obscene act in public or sings obscene songs in public shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 months or fine or both.
Whoever destroys, damages or defiles any place of worship or object held sacred with intent to insult the religion of any class shall be punished with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both.
Whoever deliberately outrages the religious feelings of any class by words or representations shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.
Whoever causes death by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide shall be punished with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both.
Whoever voluntarily causes disturbance to any assembly lawfully engaged in religious worship shall be punished with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine or both.
Whoever trespasses on burial places or offers indignity to human remains shall be punished with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine or both.

Culpable homicide is causing death by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.

Murder is culpable homicide committed with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing bodily injury known to be likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must cause death.
Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life and fine.
Whoever commits culpable homicide not amounting to murder shall be punished with imprisonment for life or up to 10 years and fine.

Where the death of a woman is caused by burns or bodily injury within 7 years of marriage and it is shown that she was subjected to cruelty for dowry, the husband or relative shall be deemed to have caused her death. Punishment: imprisonment for at least 7 years but may extend to life.
Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge that if he had caused death, it would be murder, shall be punished with imprisonment up to 10 years and fine.
Whoever attempts to commit suicide shall be punished with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine or both.
Hurt is causing bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person.

Grievous hurt includes: emasculation, permanent loss of sight, hearing, or limb, destruction of a joint, disfigurement of the head or face, fracture or dislocation of bone, or any hurt endangering life.
Whoever voluntarily causes hurt shall be punished with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine of up to Rs. 1000 or both.
Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
Punishment for voluntarily causing hurt: imprisonment up to 1 year or fine up to Rs. 1000 or both.
Punishment for voluntarily causing grievous hurt: imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means shall be punished with imprisonment for life or up to 10 years and fine.
Wrongful restraint is voluntarily obstructing any person so as to prevent him from proceeding in any direction.
Wrongful confinement is wrongfully restraining a person in such a way as to prevent him from escaping beyond certain circumscribing limits.
Whoever wrongfully restrains any person shall be punished with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine or both.
Whoever assaults or uses criminal force on any woman intending to outrage her modesty shall be punished with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both.
Sexual harassment includes unwelcome physical contact, demands for sexual favors, showing pornography, or making sexually colored remarks. Punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years or fine.
Whoever assaults or uses criminal force with intent to disrobe a woman shall be punished with imprisonment of at least 3 years but may extend to 7 years and fine.
Whoever captures or publishes images of a woman engaged in a private act without her consent shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.
Whoever follows a woman or contacts her repeatedly despite disinterest shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine.
Kidnapping is of two kinds: kidnapping from India, and kidnapping from lawful guardianship.
Kidnapping from India means conveying any person beyond the limits of India without consent.
Kidnapping from lawful guardianship means taking or enticing a minor (under 16 for males, under 18 for females) out of the keeping of their lawful guardian without consent.
Abduction is compelling a person by force to go from any place, or inducing a person to go from any place by deceitful means.
Whoever kidnaps any person shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
Whoever kidnaps or abducts a woman with intent to compel her marriage or seduce her to illicit intercourse shall be punished with imprisonment up to 10 years and fine.

A man commits rape if he engages in sexual intercourse with a woman under circumstances falling under any of six conditions: against her will, without consent, consent by fear or fraud, consent when unsound mind, with a minor under 18, or when unable to communicate consent.
Whoever commits rape shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment of at least 10 years but may extend to life imprisonment and fine. In case of gang rape, minimum 20 years imprisonment.
Whoever commits rape and causes death or persistent vegetative state shall be punished with death or rigorous imprisonment for the remainder of natural life.

Where a woman is raped by one or more persons constituting a group or acting in furtherance of a common intention, each shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment of at least 20 years, extendable to life.
Whoever voluntarily engages in carnal intercourse against the order of nature with any person shall be punished with imprisonment for life or up to 10 years and fine.
Theft is the dishonest taking of movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent.
Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.
Whoever commits theft in any building, tent or vessel used for human dwelling or custody of property shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
Whoever being a clerk or servant commits theft of property in possession of his employer shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
Whoever commits theft and causes hurt or wrongful restraint shall be punished with imprisonment up to 10 years and fine.
Extortion is putting a person in fear of injury and dishonestly inducing that person to deliver property or valuable security.
Whoever commits extortion shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.
Robbery is theft combined with causing or attempting to cause death, hurt or wrongful restraint. All theft is robbery if accompanied by such violence.
When five or more persons conjointly commit a robbery, it is dacoity.
Whoever commits robbery shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for at least 3 years but may extend to 10 years and fine.
Whoever commits dacoity shall be punished with imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and fine.
If at the time of robbery or dacoity the offender uses a deadly weapon or causes grievous hurt, the minimum imprisonment is 7 years.
Whoever dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use movable property shall be punished with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both.
Criminal breach of trust is dishonestly misappropriating or converting property entrusted to a person, or using it in violation of trust directions.
Whoever commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.
Whoever commits criminal breach of trust as a public servant, banker, merchant, agent, or broker shall be punished with imprisonment for life or up to 10 years and fine.
'Stolen property' is property obtained by theft, extortion, robbery, or criminal misappropriation, and any property obtained by dealing with such property.
Whoever dishonestly receives or retains stolen property knowing it to be stolen shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both.
Cheating is deceiving a person fraudulently or dishonestly to induce delivery of property, or to induce a person to do or omit to do something causing damage.
Cheating by personation is pretending to be another person, or substituting one person for another.
Whoever cheats shall be punished with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine or both.
Whoever cheats and dishonestly induces delivery of property shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
Mischief is causing destruction of property or any change in property destroying its value or utility.
Whoever commits mischief shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 months or fine or both.
Criminal trespass is entering into or upon property in possession of another with intent to commit an offense or to intimidate, insult or annoy.
House-trespass is criminal trespass into a building, tent or vessel used for human dwelling or worship or for custody of property.
Whoever commits criminal trespass shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 months or fine or both.
Whoever commits lurking house-trespass or house-breaking by night shall be punished with imprisonment up to 5 years and fine.
Whoever commits lurking house-trespass or house-breaking and causes hurt shall be punished with imprisonment for life or up to 10 years and fine.
Forgery is making a false document with intent to cause damage or injury, support a claim, commit fraud, or cause a person to part with property.
Whoever commits forgery shall be punished with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both.
Whoever forges a document purporting to be a valuable security, will, or authority to transfer shares shall be punished with imprisonment for life or up to 10 years and fine.
Whoever commits forgery for the purpose of cheating shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
Whoever commits forgery of a public record or court document shall be punished with imprisonment for life or up to 7 years and fine.
Whoever fraudulently uses a forged document knowing it to be forged shall be punished as if he had forged it.
Whoever, being bound by a contract to attend on a person of unsound mind, voluntarily omits to do so, shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 months or fine or both.
Whoever deceitfully causes a person to believe they are lawfully married, and cohabits with them, shall be punished with imprisonment up to 10 years and fine.
Whoever marries again during the lifetime of a spouse without the spouse being divorced shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
Whoever fraudulently goes through a marriage ceremony without the ceremony being lawful shall be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
Whoever has sexual intercourse with a married woman without the consent of her husband commits adultery.

Whoever subjects a married woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine. Cruelty includes willful conduct driving the woman to suicide or causing grave injury, and harassment for dowry.

Whoever by words spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or visible representations, makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person intending to harm their reputation, is said to defame that person.
Whoever defames another shall be punished with simple imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both.
Criminal intimidation is threatening a person with injury to their person, reputation, or property, intending to cause alarm or compel action.
Whoever intentionally insults and thereby provokes a person to break the public peace shall be punished with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both.
Whoever commits criminal intimidation shall be punished with imprisonment up to 2 years or fine or both. If the threat is to cause death or grievous hurt, imprisonment up to 7 years.

Whoever utters any word, makes any sound or gesture, or exhibits any object intending to insult the modesty of a woman, or intrudes upon her privacy, shall be punished with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine.
Whoever in a state of intoxication appears in a public place and causes annoyance shall be punished with imprisonment up to 24 hours or fine up to Rs. 10 or both.

Whoever attempts to commit an offense punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment, and does any act towards the commission of such offense, shall be punished with imprisonment up to half of the maximum imprisonment for that offense.
This Act may be called the Information Technology Act, 2000. It extends to the whole of India and applies also to any offence or contravention thereunder committed outside India by any person.

Definitions: 'Access' means gaining entry into computer resource. 'Computer' means any electronic, magnetic, optical or other high-speed data processing device. 'Cyber security' means protecting information, equipment, devices, computer resources from unauthorised access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification or destruction. 'Intermediary' means any person who on behalf of another person receives, stores or transmits electronic record.

Penalty and compensation for damage to computer system: If any person without permission of owner accesses, downloads, copies, introduces virus, damages, disrupts, denies access to computer system, he shall be liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person so affected.

Tampering with computer source documents: Whoever knowingly or intentionally conceals, destroys or alters any computer source code used for a computer, computer programme, computer system or computer network, shall be punished with imprisonment up to three years, or with fine up to two lakh rupees.

Computer related offences (Cyber Crimes & Hacking): If any person, dishonestly or fraudulently, does any act referred to in section 43, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine which may extend to five lakh rupees or with both.

Punishment for sending offensive messages through communication service (Struck Down): Section 66A was struck down as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) for violating freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).

Power to issue directions for blocking for public access of any information through any computer resource: Central Government or authorized officer may, if satisfied that it is necessary in interest of sovereignty, integrity, defense of India, security of State, friendly relations with foreign states, or public order, direct any agency/intermediary to block for access by public any information generated, transmitted, received or stored in any computer resource.

Exemption from liability of intermediary in certain cases (Safe Harbour Protection): An intermediary shall not be liable for any third party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by him if the function of the intermediary is limited to providing access to communication system and the intermediary observes due diligence while discharging duties.

nodes.title: Actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea
nodes.number: Actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea

Meaning: An act does not make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty.

Explanation: The fundamental principle of criminal law that both the physical act (actus reus) and the mental state (mens rea) must be present for a crime.

Usage: Criminal liability requires both act and intent.

nodes.title: Audi alteram partem
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Audi alteram partem

Meaning: Hear the other side.

Explanation: No person shall be condemned without being given a fair hearing. A fundamental principle of natural justice.

Usage: Both parties must be heard before any decision affecting their rights.

nodes.title: Nemo judex in causa sua
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Nemo judex in causa sua

Meaning: No one shall be a judge in their own cause.

Explanation: A person cannot be a judge in a case where they have a personal interest. This ensures impartiality and fairness in judicial proceedings.

Usage: Judges must recuse themselves if they have a conflict of interest.

nodes.title: Res ipsa loquitur
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Res ipsa loquitur

Meaning: The thing speaks for itself.

Explanation: In tort law, when an accident occurs that would not normally happen without negligence, the burden of proof shifts to the defendant.

Usage: Used in negligence cases where the cause of injury is obvious.

nodes.title: Volenti non fit injuria
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Volenti non fit injuria

Meaning: To one who consents, no wrong is done.

Explanation: A person who voluntarily consents to a risk cannot later sue for injury resulting from that risk.

Usage: Defense in tort cases where the plaintiff knowingly assumed the risk.

nodes.title: De minimis non curat lex
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: De minimis non curat lex

Meaning: The law does not concern itself with trifles.

Explanation: Minor or trivial matters are not within the concern of the law. Courts will not waste time on insignificant issues.

Usage: Used to dismiss trivial claims that do not warrant legal intervention.

nodes.title: Ubi jus ibi remedium
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Ubi jus ibi remedium

Meaning: Where there is a right, there is a remedy.

Explanation: For every legal right, there must be a corresponding legal remedy. If a person's rights are violated, the law must provide a remedy.

Usage: Ensures that rights are enforceable through legal remedies.

nodes.title: Stare decisis
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Stare decisis

Meaning: To stand by decided matters.

Explanation: Courts should follow precedents established by previous judgments. This principle ensures consistency and predictability in law.

Usage: Lower courts are bound by decisions of higher courts.

nodes.title: Ratio decidendi
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Ratio decidendi

Meaning: The reason for the decision.

Explanation: The legal principle or reasoning upon which a court's judgment is based. This is binding on lower courts as precedent.

Usage: Distinguished from obiter dicta, which are non-binding remarks.

nodes.title: Obiter dictum
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Obiter dictum

Meaning: Something said by the way.

Explanation: A remark or observation made by a judge that is not essential to the decision. Such remarks are persuasive but not binding as precedent.

Usage: Used to strengthen arguments but not binding on future courts.

nodes.title: Ex post facto
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Ex post facto

Meaning: From after the fact.

Explanation: A law that retroactively changes the legal consequences of actions committed before the law was enacted. Such laws are generally prohibited in criminal matters.

Usage: Article 20(1) of the Constitution prohibits ex post facto criminal laws.

nodes.title: Habeas corpus
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Habeas corpus

Meaning: You shall have the body.

Explanation: A writ requiring a person under arrest to be brought before a judge or into court, to prevent unlawful detention.

Usage: Article 32 and 226 — remedy against illegal detention.

nodes.title: In pari delicto
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: In pari delicto

Meaning: In equal fault.

Explanation: Where both parties are equally at fault, the law will not intervene to help either party.

Usage: Defense in contract cases where both parties have engaged in wrongdoing.

nodes.title: Caveat emptor
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Caveat emptor

Meaning: Let the buyer beware.

Explanation: The buyer is responsible for checking the quality and suitability of goods before purchase. The seller is not liable for defects the buyer could have discovered.

Usage: Principle in sale of goods, now modified by consumer protection laws.

nodes.title: Ignorantia juris non excusat
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Ignorantia juris non excusat

Meaning: Ignorance of the law is no excuse.

Explanation: A person cannot avoid liability for an offense by claiming they were unaware of the law. Everyone is presumed to know the law.

Usage: Essential for maintaining the rule of law.

nodes.title: Damnum sine injuria
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Damnum sine injuria

Meaning: Damage without legal injury.

Explanation: If a person suffers loss but no legal right is violated, there is no cause of action.

Usage: Competition causing business loss is not actionable.

nodes.title: Injuria sine damno
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Injuria sine damno

Meaning: Legal injury without damage.

Explanation: If a legal right is violated, the person can sue even if no actual loss or damage has occurred.

Usage: Trespass without actual damage is still actionable.

nodes.title: Res judicata
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Res judicata

Meaning: A matter already judged.

Explanation: A matter that has been finally adjudicated by a competent court cannot be re-litigated between the same parties.

Usage: Section 11 CPC — bars subsequent suits on same cause of action.

nodes.title: Nemo tenetur seipsum accusare
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Nemo tenetur seipsum accusare

Meaning: No one is bound to accuse themselves.

Explanation: The right against self-incrimination. A person cannot be compelled to be a witness against themselves.

Usage: Article 20(3) — right against self-incrimination.

nodes.title: Salus populi est suprema lex
nodes.content:
Legal Maxim: Salus populi est suprema lex

Meaning: The welfare of the people is the supreme law.

Explanation: The safety and welfare of the public is the highest law. In times of emergency, individual rights may be restricted for public good.

Usage: Basis for emergency powers and police power of the state.

Duty of driver in case of accident and injury to a person (Good Samaritan Protection): When any person is injured or any property damaged as a result of an accident, driver shall take all reasonable steps to secure medical attention for injured person. No Good Samaritan who voluntarily assists an accident victim shall be subjected to harassment by police or civil/criminal liability.

Necessity for insurance against third party risk: No person shall use except as a passenger, or cause or allow any other person to use, a motor vehicle in a public place, unless there is in force in relation to the use of the vehicle a policy of insurance complying with requirements of this Chapter.

Special provisions as to compensation in case of hit and run motor accident: Compensation in case of death of any person resulting from a hit and run motor accident is two lakh rupees (Rs. 2 Lakhs) and in case of grievous hurt is fifty thousand rupees (Rs. 50,000).

Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT): State Government may constitute one or more Motor Accidents Claims Tribunals for adjudicating upon claims for compensation in respect of accidents involving death or bodily injury or damage to property.

Driving dangerously: Whoever drives a motor vehicle at a speed or in a manner which is dangerous to the public shall be punished for first offence with imprisonment up to one year or fine up to five thousand rupees.

Driving by a drunken person or by a person under the influence of drugs: Whoever, while driving, or attempting to drive, a motor vehicle has in his blood alcohol exceeding 30 mg. per 100 ml. of blood detected in a test by a breath analyser shall be punished for first offence with imprisonment up to six months or fine up to ten thousand rupees.
This Act may be called the Right to Information Act, 2005. It extends to the whole of India.

Definitions: 'Public authority' means any authority or body or institution of self-government established or constituted by or under the Constitution, by any other law made by Parliament or State Legislature, or by notification issued or order made by the appropriate Government, and includes any body owned, controlled or substantially financed or non-Government organisation substantially financed, directly or indirectly by funds provided by the appropriate Government. 'Information' means any mat
Right to information: Subject to the provisions of this Act, all citizens shall have the right to information.

Obligations of public authorities: Every public authority shall maintain all its records duly catalogued and indexed, and publish within 120 days from enactment details of its organisation, functions, duties, powers of officers, decision making process, norms, rules, manuals, categories of documents held, and directory of officers (suo motu disclosure).

Request for obtaining information: A person who desires to obtain any information under this Act shall make a request in writing or through electronic means in English or Hindi or in the official language of the area, accompanying prescribed fee, to the Central Public Information Officer (CPIO) or State Public Information Officer (SPIO). An applicant making request for information shall not be required to give any reason for requesting the information or any other personal details except those t

Disposal of request: The Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer shall as expeditiously as possible, and in any case within thirty days of the receipt of the request, either provide the information on payment of fee or reject the request for any of the reasons specified in sections 8 and 9. Provided that where the information requested for concerns the life or liberty of a person, the same shall be provided within forty-eight hours of the receipt of the request.

Exemption from disclosure of information: Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, there shall be no obligation to give any citizen information affecting sovereignty and integrity of India, security, strategic or economic interests; information expressly forbidden by court; breach of privilege of Parliament; commercial confidence, trade secrets, IP unless larger public interest warrants; information available to a person in his fiduciary relationship; information received in confidence fr

Powers and functions of Information Commissions: Central Information Commission (CIC) or State Information Commission (SIC) shall receive and inquire into a complaint from any person who has been unable to submit a request because no officer has been appointed, or who has been refused information, or who believes false/incomplete info was provided.

Appeals under RTI: Any person who does not receive a decision within 30 days or is aggrieved by a decision of the CPIO/SPIO may prefer a First Appeal within 30 days to an officer senior in rank to the CPIO/SPIO. A Second Appeal against the decision shall lie within 90 days to the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission.

Penalties under RTI: Where the Information Commission at the time of deciding any complaint or appeal is of the opinion that the CPIO or SPIO has without reasonable cause refused to receive an application, delayed info without reasonable cause, or knowingly gave incorrect/misleading info, it shall impose a penalty of two hundred and fifty rupees each day till application is received or info is furnished, subject to total maximum penalty of twenty-five thousand rupees.
